short_title: Heterogeneity in blood-pressure response to 4 drugs (PHYSIC repeated crossover trial)

citation.title: Heterogeneity in Blood Pressure Response to 4 Antihypertensive Drugs: A Randomized Clinical Trial

access.full_text_source: PubMed Central article page (PMC10091169), converted to text; figure images not inspected

study.design_detail: Randomized, double-blind, repeated crossover trial (PHYSIC, NCT02774460). After a 2-week placebo run-in, each participant had 6 treatment periods in random order: one each of lisinopril 20 mg, candesartan 16 mg, hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg and amlodipine 10 mg, plus repeats of 2 randomly chosen drugs. Periods of 7-9 weeks (half dose weeks 1-2) separated by 1-week placebo washouts. Mixed-effects models estimated average contrasts and between-person variation in contrasts; repeated crossovers tested whether a person's response replicated.
study.population: Men and women aged 40-75 with grade 1 hypertension at low cardiovascular risk, untreated or on monotherapy that could be stopped; office SBP 140-179 mm Hg at randomization; exclusions included diabetes, cardiovascular disease and kidney failure. 54% men, mean age 64
study.setting: Single outpatient research clinic, Uppsala University Hospital, Sweden; screening 2017-2020, last visit June 2021
study.exposure_or_intervention: Lisinopril, candesartan, hydrochlorothiazide and amlodipine monotherapy at fixed doses
study.comparator: Each of the other three drugs (all 6 pairwise contrasts), within the same participant
outcomes: Daytime (10:00-20:00) ambulatory systolic blood pressure at the end of each treatment period
study.follow_up: About a year per participant: 6 treatment periods (median 56 days) with washouts

findings_summary: In a randomized, double-blind repeated crossover trial (280 randomized; 1468 treatment periods analysed in 270), people differed in which antihypertensive drug lowered their daytime ambulatory systolic blood pressure most. For four drug pairs the between-person SD of the treatment difference was 7.2-8.9 mm Hg, and a participant's first crossover difference predicted their repeat crossover difference. For lisinopril vs candesartan and hydrochlorothiazide vs amlodipine, large person-level differences were excluded. Compared with always using lisinopril (on average the most effective drug at the doses used), personalized single-drug choice would lower SBP by an estimated 3.1 mm Hg on average; the headline 4.4 mm Hg is a theoretical maximum against a fixed choice if the drugs had been equipotent on average. Both are model-based estimates that assume each person's response is known exactly.

limitations.text: Single centre, specific population (grade 1 hypertension, low risk, Swedish clinic) and four specific drugs at fixed doses; generalizability is uncertain. The authors note the run-in and single-centre design could lead to an underestimation of heterogeneity.
The estimand is biologic efficacy variation among adherent participants (primary analysis: periods with at least 90% adherence); effects under real-world adherence may differ.
The doses were not equipotent on average for some pairs.
Some non-adherence; monotherapy only, whereas many guidelines start with combination therapy.

The personalization gains assume each person's true treatment contrast is known; the repeat-crossover slopes (about 0.1-0.7) show a single observed comparison identifies it only with substantial noise.
The 4.4 and 3.1 mm Hg gains are model-based estimates of potential benefit under the fitted model, not benefits demonstrated by assigning personalized treatment and measuring the result.
The outcome is blood pressure, a surrogate; the trial does not measure cardiovascular events.
The authors note the year-long identification process used in the trial is not proposed for each patient.
Supplement (eTables 6-10, sensitivity analyses) and figure images were not reviewed for this record.

applicability_constraints: Adults 40-75 with grade 1 hypertension at low cardiovascular risk, eligible to stop current therapy; diabetes, cardiovascular disease and kidney failure excluded.
Drug-response findings apply to these drugs and doses under trial conditions with ambulatory measurement; they say nothing about behavioural interventions.
Medication choice is outside this project's authority; the relevance here is measurement and design, not drug selection.

discrepancies.description: For hydrochlorothiazide vs amlodipine the between-person SD was 2.4 mm Hg (95% CI 1.1-3.9; P < .001), i.e. small heterogeneity was statistically present, while the Discussion speaks of the 'absence of a potential for benefit' for this pair; a heteroscedastic sensitivity model gave somewhat larger variation for this pair.
discrepancies.handling: Record says large personal differences were excluded for this pair, not that heterogeneity was absent.

interpretation: This is direct, randomized evidence that the average response can misdescribe individuals for some drug pairs, and that a person's response can replicate when measured carefully and repeatedly. It also shows what that took: ambulatory monitoring at the end of each period, washouts, blinding, and repeated periods to separate a consistent personal response from within-person noise, which the authors describe as generally larger than drug-titration effects. The estimated personalization benefit is conditional on the model and was not tested prospectively. For this project, the transferable lesson is about measurement design for any future behavioural comparison, not about medication.

review.verified_by: Automated agent (Claude) during an unattended session; not an independent or clinical review
review.method: Each reported value was matched against a verbatim quote from the PMC full text (Table 2 rows and Results sentences), and each quote was checked against the cached full text by evidence_tools.validate. Citation metadata was checked against the PubMed record. Derived pairwise gains use the formula stated in the Methods and are labelled as our calculations.
